extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors / patent attorneys and agents using USPTO examiner data (Patent Bots users)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent prosecutors on how to interpret and use Patent Bots examiner statistics (grant rates, timelines, interview benefit, appeals history) to inform prosecution decisions (interview, amend, RCE, appeal, abandon). Focused on U.S. patent prosecution and examiner-specific behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-year grant rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of the examiner's applications that are granted at 3 years after the first office action (referred to repeatedly as the '3-year' grant rate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary metric for comparing examiner difficulty. Use it to set client expectations (e.g., tell a client their chance of an issued patent in 3 years), and as an input to decide whether to amend claims, spend more time on quality arguments, or take more aggressive actions like appeals. The blog notes advantages of the 3-year grant rate over a conventional grant rate (see separate post).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty ranking / percentile
rubrics_metrics.description: Rank of an examiner among all USPTO examiners according to their grant rate, shown as a percentile (e.g., '92nd percentile' meaning harder than 92% of examiners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translates grant rate into an easy-to-understand difficulty label (e.g., 'extremely hard'). Use it to calibrate strategy: with a harder examiner, set expectations, prepare to amend claims, or focus on higher-quality arguments; with an easier examiner, be less inclined to amend and instead argue for allowance of as-filed claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment information (group, tech classes, degree, contact, location)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary of examiner's group, technology classes, degree, contact information, and location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to assess how likely the examiner is to understand the invention (e.g., advanced degree for complicated tech is helpful), detect misclassification (may need to do more work to get the examiner to appreciate the invention), and to schedule interviews (OA usually lacks email/location).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant-rate timeline (percent granted/pending/abandoned over time)
rubrics_metrics.description: A timeline graph showing for each month after the first office action the percentage of cases that are granted, pending, and abandoned; the 3-year grant rate is the value at 3 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for setting client expectations and concisely summarizing examiner behavior over time. Helps identify how examiner behavior changes as prosecution progresses and informs decisions about when to file an RCE, file a notice of appeal, or abandon. The timeline supports classification of examiners into behavioral types (master, ideologue, decider, negotiator, granter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to art unit and USPTO average
rubrics_metrics.description: Bar chart comparing the examiner's grant rate to his/her art unit and the USPTO average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps determine whether an examiner is much harder or easier than their peers. If much harder than the art unit average, this can be used to seek sympathy from a supervisor or may increase chances with a pre-appeal conference request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview benefit (grant rate with vs without applicant-requested interviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two grant rates: (1) over cases that had no applicant-requested interviews and (2) over cases with at least one applicant-requested interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure of whether interviewing the examiner improves outcomes. For most examiners, interview increases grant rate, but exceptions exist where grant rate is lower for interviewed cases — in those cases you may be better off skipping the interview. Use this to decide whether to request an interview after an office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interview tendency (frequency of interviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator of how often an examiner conducts applicant-requested interviews (some examiners almost never do interviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner rarely does interviews, requesting one may be futile; consider skipping the request. Use interview frequency along with interview benefit to decide versus invest time requesting interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recent dispositions (counts of granted and abandoned cases over past 6 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of an examiner's granted and abandoned cases over the past 6 years and a list of recent cases that were granted or abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful because an examiner's grant rate can change over time (e.g., increases upon promotion to primary examiner, or due to changes in law such as 35 U.S.C. §101). Use recent trends to inform whether to file an RCE (if grant rate recently improved) or to appeal. Reviewing recent allowed cases helps identify persuasive arguments and can inform responses (particularly for 101 rejections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of office-action rejection details (OA Rejections column / case-level office actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each case, Patent Bots shows a list of office actions and the rejections contained in each one (OA Rejections column available with Premium Statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saves time by letting you jump directly to office actions that contain the specific rejection you face. Use these examples to study how other attorneys overcame the same rejection and to craft similar arguments in your response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to image file wrapper (PatentPlex link to download office actions/responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Button/link to take you directly to PatentPlex image file wrapper pages to download office actions and responses (separate subscription).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes retrieving the full prosecution record easy without going to PAIR; useful for deep review of examiner's allowed/rejected cases and for preparing responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals statistics (overall outcome, PTAB decision, pre-appeal outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics for three appeals-related events: (1) the overall outcome of the appeal (at least 1 claim granted, all claims rejected, or prosecution reopened), (2) for fully briefed appeals the PTAB decision (examiner affirmed, affirmed in part, or reversed), and (3) the outcome of a pre-appeal conference (proceed to appeal, prosecution reopened, or claims allowed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine appeals statistics with grant rate to inform appeal decisions. For example, a high chance of claims allowed on appeal suggests appealing; detailed PTAB outcomes inform whether appeals are generally reversed or affirmed for this examiner, affecting whether to appeal early or pursue other options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using combined grant-rate and appeal outcomes to choose strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative decision rules linking grant rate and appeal outcomes to prosecution options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: (a) examiner with low grant rate who is often affirmed on appeal — consider abandoning or filing a continuation to seek a different examiner; (b) examiner with low grant rate who is often reversed on appeal — appeal early (possibly after first final action); (c) examiner with high grant rate who is often affirmed on appeal — file an RCE and work to reach compromise with the examiner. Use these heuristics as part of case-level strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals history (case-level docket and color-coded outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of all the examiner's appeals with a brief docket of appeal events and color coding for outcomes (at least one claim granted, all claims rejected, or prosecution reopened).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal history tells you what actually happened in each appeal. Distinguish between claims allowed because the examiner changed their mind before the Board versus allowances that followed a Board reversal — allowances before a Board decision mean faster allowance and may make appeals more attractive. Use the appeal history to predict likely timelines and probabilities for successful appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner behavioral taxonomy from grant-rate timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of examiners into different behavioral types based on their grant-rate timeline (the blog references five types: the master, the ideologue, the decider, the negotiator, and the granter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing an examiner's type helps tailor prosecution strategy (e.g., when to file RCE, appeal, or abandon). The grant-rate timeline is the data source for identifying these types; use the taxonomy to infer how the examiner typically handles cases over time and to optimize interactions (interviews, arguments, amendments).
